title: Look-Ahead Bias, Transaction Costs and Slippage
objectives: Identify look-ahead bias in a backtest design and apply the signal-execute-next-bar fix
Compute per-side and round-trip transaction costs from spread, commission and impact
Quantify the effect of costs on a strategy's edge in basis points
Explain slippage and how live fills diverge from backtest assumptions
motivation: Two innocent assumptions, 'I can trade at the price my signal used' and 'trading is free', account for the majority of backtests that collapse in production. The signal uses today's close to buy at today's close, which requires knowing the close before it prints. Then every trade pays real costs that the simulation skipped. This lesson builds the discipline of time-safe signals and honest cost modelling.

blocks.text: Look-ahead bias: the time machine in your loop

blocks.caption: Lookahead is negative latency: free microseconds you will not get in production.

blocks.md: The classic pattern: compute a signal from today's close, then simulate the fill *at today's close*. In live trading the close is not knowable until it prints, the signal and the fill race each other, and reality loses. Variants are sneakier: using a restated fundamental (published later) on its original date, using today's volume profile to time an intraday entry, or normalising features with statistics computed over the whole sample (a full-sample mean is future information to a 2015 data point).

blocks.title: The fix, shown on three days
items: Day 1 close: \$100.00; the signal (computed from day 1 data) says buy.
**Biased fill**: buy at \$100.00 on day 1, impossible in reality.
**Honest fill**: buy at day 2's open, which here is \$101.00 - you pay the overnight gap of $+1\%$ whenever a signal fires before an up-open.
The honest backtest must decide the position from data up to day 1 and execute at the *next tradable price*. One bar of delay is the price of not clairvoying.
Expect honest results to look worse, a strategy whose edge survives next-bar execution is the only kind worth having.

blocks.title: Subtle look-ahead checklist
blocks.md: Signals that use same-bar high/low for stop logic; volatilities estimated including the current bar; machine-learning features scaled with full-sample statistics; event studies using the announcement-day close to 'decide'. Each one leaks the future. Audit: for any timestamp $t$, could every input to the decision have been known strictly before the fill time?

Look-ahead bias is the single most efficient way to manufacture a profitable backtest: use one piece of information from the future, and the strategy looks brilliant forever. Its cousin, the same-bar assumption (compute the signal from the 15:59:59 close and also trade at that close), is subtler and even more common, it hides inside innocent-looking indexing like `df['signal'] = df['close'] > df['close'].rolling(20).mean()` followed by `df['pnl'] = df['signal'] * df['ret']` where `ret` is the *same* bar's return.

blocks.title: The one-line audit for same-bar leakage
items: Write the timeline explicitly: at 15:59:59 the bar closes; the signal needs the close; execution needs the signal. Execution therefore cannot happen at 15:59:59. The earliest honest execution is the next bar's open (plus your latency).

The audit rule: **the return you book for bar $t$ must use prices from bar $t+1$ onwards.** In pandas: `signal.shift(1) * ret`, and if you trade the open, `ret` itself must be open-to-open, not close-to-close.

Typical magnitudes (illustrative): an intraday reversal strategy leaking one close-to-open gap can gain 50 to 200bp of annual alpha from that leak alone, on a strategy whose real edge is zero. The gap between "backtest Sharpe 1.8" and "live Sharpe −0.2" is usually one `shift(1)`.

Transaction costs enter the same audit: your fill assumption must include the spread you would actually cross, at the size you would actually trade, in the liquidity that existed *at that moment*, historical spread data exists precisely for this line of the budget.

blocks.title: Walk-forward as structural honesty
blocks.md: The cure that also proves the medicine: re-run the entire pipeline (normalisation, calibration, everything) in a rolling walk-forward where each month's parameters come only from prior months. If performance collapses versus the full-sample backtest, the difference *was* leakage and snooping, quantified for free. The walk-forward number is the one honest estimate of live performance you can produce before going live.
Every side of every trade pays three components. Take a hypothetical liquid stock with a 10bp spread, 3bp commission and 7bp expected impact for your order size:

blocks.title: Cost arithmetic, in basis points of notional
items: **Per side**: half-spread $= 10/2 = 5$bp (you cross the spread once), commission $= 3$bp, impact $= 7$bp. Total per side $= 5 + 3 + 7 = 15$bp.
**Round trip** (buy then later sell): $2 \times 15 = 30$bp of notional.
A strategy whose gross edge is 40bp per round trip nets $40 - 30 = 10$bp, a $75\%$ haircut on the edge.
At 50 round trips per year on \$10m average notional, costs alone are $50 \times 0.0030 \times 10{,}000{,}000 = $1{,}500{,}000$ per year. Costs scale with turnover, not with profit.

blocks.md: Implications that reshape research: high-turnover strategies need enormous gross edges; cost-aware signal design prefers fewer, larger, more patient trades; and cost estimates must be size-dependent, a \$5m order in a thin name pays far more than 7bp of impact. Model costs as a function of size, spread and volatility (the square-root law from the microstructure module is a standard backbone), never as a flat constant.

blocks.text: Slippage: where the live P&L leaks

blocks.md: Slippage is the difference between the price your system *assumed* and the price it *got*. Backtest assumes fill at signal close \$100.00; the live order, racing through the same decision a millisecond later, fills at \$100.06, 6bp of slippage on that trade. Sources: latency between signal and order arrival, adverse moves while the order works, partial fills at worse levels, and the market moving because of your own order. Production systems log expected-vs-executed per fill; the aggregate is a KPI called **implementation shortfall**, the all-in cost of getting from intention to position.

blocks.title: The two-question audit for any backtest
blocks.md: (1) Time-safety: is every decision input known strictly before the fill timestamp? (2) Cost-honesty: is every fill charged a size-aware cost? If either answer is no, the reported Sharpe is a property of the simulation, not of the strategy. Everything in the next lesson, overfitting aside, builds on getting these two right first.

guidedExercise.prompt: A strategy trades monthly with a gross expected edge of 60bp per round trip. Costs: spread 12bp, commission 4bp, impact 6bp, all per side. (a) Compute the per-side and round-trip costs. (b) Net edge per round trip. (c) If turnover doubles (twice as many round trips on the same notional), what happens to the net annual edge per unit of notional traded, and what does that imply about turnover?
hints: Costs scale with the *number* of trades; edge is per round trip.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) Per side $= 6 + 4 + 6 = 16$bp; round trip $= 32$bp. (b) Net edge $= 60 - 32 = 28$bp per round trip. (c) Doubling turnover doubles total cost per unit of notional (from 32bp to 64bp of cost per two round trips) while the gross edge per round trip stays 60bp, the *average* net edge per round trip is unchanged but total net P&L rises only if the extra trades carry the same edge; if marginal trades have weaker edge, more turnover can subtract value. Turnover must be justified by edge, not by activity.

independentExercise.prompt: An intraday strategy fires 200 times per year on \$2m notional per round trip. Gross edge: 25bp per round trip. Costs: 8bp spread, 2bp commission, 5bp impact (per side). (a) Round-trip cost in bp. (b) Net edge per round trip in bp and in dollars per trade. (c) Annual net P&L in dollars. (d) The live system measures 3bp average slippage per side beyond assumptions, recompute (c).
independentExercise.solution: (a) Per side $= 4 + 2 + 5 = 11$bp; round trip $= 22$bp. (b) Net $= 25 - 22 = 3$bp per round trip $= 3 \times $200 = \$6$ per trade. (c) $200 \times 600 = $120{,}000$ per year. (d) Extra cost $= 6$bp per round trip $= $1{,}200$; net edge $= -3$bp $= -\$6$ per trade $\Rightarrow -$120{,}000$ per year: slippage alone flipped the strategy from profitable to losing.

commonMistakes: Filling at the same bar's close that generated the signal, the textbook look-ahead error.
Using full-sample statistics (means, scalers, model fits) inside features that must be causal at each date.
Modelling costs as a flat constant regardless of order size, venue or volatility.
Comparing backtest Sharpe to live Sharpe without an implementation-shortfall accounting, the gap is usually costs plus slippage, not bad luck.
realWorldApplication: Best-execution regulation (MiFID II, Reg NMS) obliges brokers to measure implementation shortfall; quant funds routinely discover that a 'profitable' paper strategy's live P&L equals paper P&L minus exactly the cost-plus-slippage model this lesson computes.
quantFinanceApplication: Execution engines store per-fill expected-vs-actual prices, attribute slippage to latency/impact/adverse-move buckets, and feed the measured costs back into the backtester's cost model, closing the loop between simulation and production.
summary: Look-ahead bias = any decision input not knowable before the fill time; the fix is decide-on-$t$, execute-on-$t+1$ timing.
Per-side cost $=$ half-spread $+$ commission $+$ size-aware impact; round trips pay double.
Costs scale with turnover: a 40bp gross edge became a 10bp net edge in the worked example.
Slippage is the live gap between assumed and actual fills; implementation shortfall is its aggregated, all-in measure.

quiz.prompt: A backtest computes a signal from Friday's close and fills the order at Friday's close. The correct fix is to:
options: Decide from Friday's data and fill at the next tradable price (e.g. Monday's open)
Compute the signal from Monday's close
Fill at Friday's close only if the signal is strong
quiz.explanation: The close is unknowable until it prints, so a decision made from it cannot also fill at it; the honest fill happens at the next executable price, paying the overnight gap when it goes against you.

quiz.prompt: Spread 10bp, commission 3bp, impact 7bp, all per side. Round-trip cost in bp?
Gross edge 40bp per round trip, round-trip cost 30bp. Net edge in bp?
Which of these are look-ahead bias?
options: Normalising features with a mean computed over the entire sample
Using a restated earnings figure on its original announcement date
Filling at the open of the day after the signal
Estimating volatility including the bar on which the trade decision is made
quiz.explanation: All three leak future information into past decisions; (2) is the honest next-bar design. Restatements must be used with their *revision* dates, not original dates.

quiz.prompt: Backtest assumes a fill at \$100.00; live fill is \$100.06. Slippage in bp?
quiz.explanation: $0.06/100.00 = 0.0006 = 6$bp, logged per fill and aggregated as implementation shortfall.

quiz.prompt: Why should impact costs be modelled as a function of order size rather than a flat rate?
quiz.modelAnswer: Impact grows with size relative to available depth and daily volume (square-root-law behaviour), so a flat rate undercharges large orders in thin names and overcharges small ones; size-aware models let research compare slicing plans and honest net edges.
quiz.explanation: The cost of trading depends on how much of the book you consume, a constant silently breaks both of those cases.

flashcards.back: Using information in a backtest decision that was not knowable at the fill time; the fix is decide-at-$t$, fill-at-next-tradable-price.
Half-spread $+$ commission $+$ impact; round trip $= 2 \times$ per side.
Difference between the fill price the system assumed and the price actually obtained, aggregated as implementation shortfall.

flashcards.front: Why do high-turnover strategies suffer most from costs?
flashcards.back: Costs are paid per trade while edge is earned per trade, costs scale linearly with turnover, so thin edges are consumed fastest.
